Title: Current and Future Development in Lung Cancer Diagnosis.
Abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in North America and other developed countries. One of the reasons lung cancer is at the top of the list is that it is often not diagnosed until the cancer is at an advanced stage. Thus, the earliest diagnosis of lung cancer is crucial, especially in screening high-risk populations, such as smokers, exposure to fumes, oil fields, toxic occupational places, etc. Based on the current knowledge, it looks that there is an urgent need to identify novel biomarkers. The current diagnosis of lung cancer includes different types of imaging complemented with pathological assessment of biopsies, but these techniques can still not detect early lung cancer developments. In this review, we described the advantages and disadvantages of current methods used in diagnosing lung cancer, and we provide an analysis of the potential use of body fluids as carriers of biomarkers as predictors of cancer development and progression.
Abstract_Summary: This research paper looks at how we can find lung cancer early, before it grows and spreads (Abstract, sentence 2). Lung cancer causes more deaths than any other cancer in rich countries like the United States and Canada (Abstract, sentence 1). This work may help people who smoke or who work around fumes, oil fields, or other toxic places (Abstract, sentence 3). Today, we use scans and small tissue samples from the lung to find cancer, but these tests often miss very early lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 5). The writers of this paper review how these tests work and where they fall short (Abstract, sentence 6). They say we need new “markers,” which are signs in the body that can warn us when cancer may be starting (Abstract, sentence 4). The team looks at body fluids, like blood or spit, as easy ways to carry these warning signs (Abstract, sentence 6). If we can find strong and clear markers in these fluids, we may be able to test people at high risk more often and catch cancer sooner (Abstract, sentence 3). In the future, this may lead to simple lab tests that help you and your doctor find lung cancer at an early stage (Abstract, sentence 6).
Full_Text_Summary_With_In_Text_Citations: This research looks at better ways to find lung cancer early, before it has spread and is hard to treat (Abstract, para. 1). We need this work because lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death, and most people are found when the disease is already at stage 3 or 4 (Introduction, para. 1). If you smoke or have breathed in fumes at work, early tests could help you get care sooner (Introduction, para. 2). The authors review current tests like chest scans and scope exams of the airways, and they explain how these can miss small, early tumors or give many false alarms (Introduction, para. 3). They then look at new lab tests that use body fluids such as blood, spit, and urine to search for “biomarkers,” which are cancer signals in these fluids (Introduction, para. 4). They report that some blood and spit markers can tell people with lung cancer from healthy people, even in early stages, but single markers are often not accurate enough by themselves (Body, para. 41). New ideas include blood tests, urine tests, and breath‑related tests that may work together with scans to guide who needs a biopsy and who does not (Methods, para. 5). If future studies confirm these fluid tests, you may one day have a simple blood or urine test to help find lung cancer earlier and with less pain and cost (Conclusion, para. 3).
